title: Interactive Connectivity Establishment (ICE)
summary: Describes Interactive Connectivity Establishment, a way to get through NATs for UDP media sessions set up with the offer/answer model. It uses STUN and TURN to try several routes and choose a working one, and it can be used with protocols like SIP. It was replaced by RFC 8445 and RFC 8839. It is a standards-track specification.

eli5.summary: Two people behind locked doors try many paths to meet and pick one that works. ICE tries addresses and relay options to connect calls.

subtitle: How two endpoints behind NATs gather, test and choose a working network path for a UDP media session.

tldr.problem: Protocols that use the offer/answer model carry IP addresses and ports in their messages and want media to flow directly between peers, which is hard when one or both sides are behind NATs.
tldr.mechanism: Each agent gathers several candidate transport addresses (local, NAT-translated and relayed), sends them in the SDP offer and answer, then tests candidate pairs with STUN connectivity checks in priority order and picks one that works.
tldr.outcome: RFC 5245 is obsoleted by RFC 8445 and RFC 8839, and it was updated by RFC 6336. New work should follow the newer documents.

today: RFC 5245 has been obsoleted by RFC 8445 and RFC 8839, and it was updated by RFC 6336, so it is no longer the current ICE specification. It is a Proposed Standard that obsoleted RFC 4091 and RFC 4092.

sections.title: The NAT Problem ICE Solves
sections.content:
RFC 3264 defines a two-phase exchange of Session Description Protocol (SDP) messages, the offer/answer model, used by protocols such as SIP. These protocols are hard to run through Network Address Translators (NATs) because they carry the IP addresses and ports of media sources inside their messages. They also try to create a media flow directly between participants, to reduce latency and packet loss and to lower operating costs.

Many fixes already existed, among them application layer gateways, the Middlebox Control Protocol, the original STUN and Realm Specific IP. The RFC says each one is best in some network topologies and poor in others, so operators end up making brittle assumptions about their networks. What is needed is a single flexible solution.

Interactive Connectivity Establishment (ICE) is that solution for UDP-based media streams set up with offer/answer. It extends offer/answer by putting many IP addresses and ports into the SDP, then testing them with peer-to-peer connectivity checks. The checks use the revised STUN specification, and ICE also uses TURN. Because it handles several addresses per stream, it also helps multihomed and dual-stack hosts, and for that reason it deprecates RFC 4091 and RFC 4092.
sections.eli5: When both friends are behind locked gates, telling each other your address is not enough. ICE gives a whole list of possible doors and checks which ones open.

sections.title: Candidates and How They Are Gathered
sections.content:
An agent is one endpoint. Each agent collects candidates, which are transport addresses (an IP address plus a UDP port) it might use to talk to its peer. There are three kinds defined here:

  • A host candidate comes straight from a local network interface, including VPN or other tunnel interfaces.
  • A server reflexive candidate is the translated address on the public side of a NAT, learned from a STUN or TURN server.
  • A relayed candidate is an address allocated on a TURN server, which forwards traffic between the agents.

A fourth type, the peer reflexive candidate, is not gathered up front. It is discovered during connectivity checks when a STUN response shows a translated address the agent did not already know.

The base of a candidate is the address the agent sends from for it. A host candidate is its own base. If an agent is not behind a NAT, its server reflexive candidate equals its base and is redundant, so it is eliminated. When there are several NATs between the agent and the TURN server, only the outermost server reflexive address is discovered.

Each candidate also gets a foundation: candidates share one when they are the same type, have bases with the same IP address, use STUN or TURN servers with the same IP address (for reflexive and relayed ones) and use the same transport protocol.
sections.eli5: A candidate is one possible door to your house: the front door you can see, the door your neighbourhood gate shows to outsiders, or a door at a helper's office who passes messages along.

sections.title: Prioritizing Candidates
sections.content:
Every candidate for a media stream gets a unique priority, a positive integer between 1 and 2**31 - 1. Agents SHOULD use the recommended formula so that both sides order their checks in a coordinated way; with a different formula ICE takes longer to converge.

priority = (2^24)*(type preference) +
           (2^8)*(local preference) +
           (2^0)*(256 - component ID)

The type preference is an integer from 0 to 126, where 126 is the highest and 0 means last resort only. The local preference is an integer from 0 to 65535 that ranks the agent's own IP addresses when it is multihomed; with a single address it SHOULD be 65535. The component ID is between 1 and 256 (for RTP-based streams, RTP is component 1 and RTCP is component 2).

The aim is that more direct routes, with fewer relays and NATs, are preferred. Relayed candidates add latency, can add packet loss and cost the provider money, so their type preference SHOULD be lower than that of host candidates. After sorting, the local and remote priorities are combined so that both agents order the candidate pairs identically. This matters because NATs often refuse incoming packets until the host behind them has sent one outward.
sections.eli5: You rank your doors from best to worst: the closest door first, the door at the helper's office last. Both friends use the same ranking, so they end up knocking on matching doors at the same time.

sections.title: Connectivity Checks and Nomination
sections.content:
After exchanging candidates in the SDP offer and answer, each agent pairs local and remote candidates into candidate pairs and sorts them into a check list. It then sends a STUN request on each pair in priority order, and acknowledges requests from the other side. When both agents check the same pair the result is a four-message handshake. The STUN requests go to and from the same addresses and ports that carry media, so agents tell STUN and RTP/RTCP apart by packet contents, not by port. As an optimization, a triggered check is sent as soon as an agent receives a check from its peer on a pair.

To avoid repeated tests of pairs likely to fail, pairs that share a foundation are held in the Frozen state. Only pairs with unique foundations start out testable, and when one succeeds the others with the same foundation are unfrozen. A pair is always in one of Frozen, Waiting, In-Progress, Succeeded or Failed.

One agent is the controlling agent and the other is the controlled agent. The controlling agent nominates the pair to use. With regular nomination it waits for at least one valid pair per media stream, picks one and sends a second STUN request carrying a flag. With aggressive nomination it sets the flag in every request, so the first success ends processing; that is faster but less flexible. The pair in use for media is the selected pair. If the default candidates in the SDP do not match the selected ones, the controlling agent sends an updated offer, and either agent can restart ICE with an updated offer.
sections.eli5: The friends take turns knocking on matching doors. Once one pair of doors lets both sides through, the leader says that is the one, and everyone stops knocking.

sections.title: Security of the Checks
sections.content:
Because ICE decides where media is sent, it must not be hijackable. Each STUN connectivity check is protected by a message authentication code computed with a key exchanged in the signaling channel (the SDP carries ice-ufrag and ice-pwd), so an attacker cannot forge or modify checks without that key. This only helps if the signaling itself is protected, so ICE is meant to be used with secure signaling such as SIPS.

The RFC lists attacks that try to make an agent believe something false: a valid pair is marked invalid, an invalid pair is marked valid, or a false peer reflexive candidate is accepted, which could redirect media to a denial-of-service target or to an eavesdropper. As a countermeasure, an agent MUST limit the total number of connectivity checks it performs, with a configurable limit and a default of 100 recommended.
sections.eli5: The friends share a secret password through their trusted messenger, and every knock has to include it. A stranger who does not know the password cannot trick them into opening the wrong door.

sections.title: Keepalives, Lite Agents and Deployment
sections.content:
All endpoints MUST send keepalives for each media session to keep NAT bindings alive, even when ICE is not used. If no packet has been sent on the selected pair for Tr seconds, a keepalive is required. Tr SHOULD be configurable with a default of 15 seconds, and MUST NOT be configured below 15 seconds. Full ICE agents talking to an ICE peer MUST use STUN Binding Indications for this.

ICE defines two kinds of implementation. A full implementation does everything described above. A lite implementation is meant for devices that always have a public IP address: it only offers host candidates, sends no checks, and only responds to them. It includes the a=ice-lite attribute in its SDP. When a full agent meets a lite agent, the full agent is controlling. The lite mode was added as a stepping stone, and a full implementation is preferable where possible.

ICE was designed to work with existing NATs and firewalls without reconfiguring them. It works best with NATs that follow the recommendations of RFC 4787 and RFC 5766, and in such networks it works without a TURN server, which improves voice quality and call setup time.
sections.eli5: Once the path is found, the friends wave to each other every so often so the gate guard does not lock that door again. A helper who never moves can skip the knocking game and just answer when someone knocks.
